q-66256.name: Question 1
q-66256.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14208916/assets/8c884e34e0fd8b310984c2197ff0ea606033d00d63a0c6e0e04f0c993f519755.png)

The function $f(x)$ is represented by the mapping diagram above. What is ${f}^{-1}(4)?$
q-66256.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The function ${f}^{-1}(x)$ reverses the action of $f(x),$ as depicted below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14208916/assets/a0194a90466532c723c904d5ef9fea394e976b8b1f5287f066d5843f575e762e.png)

 

From the above, we see that ${f}^{-1}(4)=5.$

**Method 2**

From the given mapping diagram, we have:

$$
f(5)=4
$$

Applying ${f}^{-1}$ to both sides of the above equation, and using the fact that ${f}^{-1}(f(x))=x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(f(5)) & ={f}^{-1}(4) \\ 5 & ={f}^{-1}(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that ${f}^{-1}(4)=5.$

q-78657.name: Question 4
q-78657.problem:
Given that

$$
g(-\sqrt{2})=4,\,g(\sqrt{3})=-7,\,g(4)=-6,
$$

find the value of ${g}^{-1}(4).$
q-78657.worked_solution:
From the given information, we have:

$$
g(-\sqrt{2})=4
$$

Applying ${g}^{-1}$ to both sides of the above equation, and using the fact that ${g}^{-1}(g(x))=x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{-1}(g(-\sqrt{2})) & ={g}^{-1}(4) \\ -\sqrt{2} & ={g}^{-1}(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that ${g}^{-1}(4)=-\sqrt{2}.$

q-158082.name: Question 7
q-158082.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=x-10$ and $g(x)=x+k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
q-158082.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =x+k \\ g(f(x)) & =f(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=x-10$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =f(x)+k \\  & =x-10+k \\  & =x-10+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-10+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-10+k & =\cancel{x} \\ -10+k & =0 \\ k & =10\end{aligned}
$$

q-34814.name: Question 8
q-34814.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=\frac{x}{3}+7$ and $g(x)=3x+k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
q-34814.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace everxy occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =3x+k \\ g(f(x)) & =3f(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=\frac{x}{3}+7$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =3f(x)+k \\  & =3(\frac{x}{3}+7)+k \\  & =x+21+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+21+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}+21+k & =\cancel{x} \\ 21+k & =0 \\ k & =-21\end{aligned}
$$

q-158088.name: Question 9
q-158088.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=\frac{x}{8}$ and $g(x)=kx.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
q-158088.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =kx \\ g(f(x)) & =kf(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=\frac{x}{8}$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =kf(x) \\  & =k(\frac{x}{8}) \\  & =\frac{k}{8}x\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{8}x & =x \\ \frac{k}{8}\cancel{x} & =\cancel{x} \\ \frac{k}{8} & =1 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$
